questions.question: Why do Darwin's four observations (variation, overproduction, struggle, differential survival) NECESSARILY produce evolution?
questions.solution: More offspring are produced than survive; heritable variation exists; those whose variation fits the environment survive and reproduce more. Their variants become common in the next generation — allele frequencies change. Given those premises, evolution follows by logic: selection is the non-random survival of random variation.

questions.concept: Selection acts on phenotypes, evolution on gene pools
questions.question: Why is it wrong to say 'giraffes stretched their necks and their offspring inherited longer necks' (Lamarck)?
questions.solution: Acquired traits (stretched muscles) do not change DNA in the germ line — only genetic changes in eggs/sperm are heritable. Selection cannot CREATE a longer neck by need; it can only FAVOUR individuals whose genes already gave a slightly longer neck. Mechanism of inheritance, not intent, decides what evolves.

questions.question: Distinguish homologous from analogous organs and say what each type of evidence supports.
questions.solution: Homologous: same basic structure, different function (human arm, whale flipper, bat wing — same bones) → COMMON ANCESTRY (divergent evolution). Analogous: same function, different structure (insect wing vs bird wing) → CONVERGENT evolution, similar selection pressures on unrelated bodies. Homology traces family trees; analogy shows selection's power to shape similar solutions independently.

questions.question: Why did dark (melanic) peppered moths replace light ones in industrial England, then reverse after clean-air laws?
questions.solution: On soot-darkened trees, light moths were eaten more by birds — dark variants survived and reproduced, so the melanic allele spread. Clean-air laws restored lichen-covered light bark; selection flipped, light moths again survived better. The allele's frequency tracks the environment — selection is directional and reversible.

questions.question: Why does geographic isolation usually precede the formation of new species?
questions.solution: Separated populations stop exchanging genes; different mutations, drift and selection accumulate independently. Over time, even if they meet again, they may not interbreed successfully — reproductive isolation, the criterion of species. Gene flow homogenises; isolation lets divergence happen.

questions.question: An individual organism can grow stronger or faster, but populations evolve. Why must evolution be defined at population level?
questions.solution: Evolution is a change in ALLELE FREQUENCIES across generations. An individual's lifetime change is not inherited and does not alter the gene pool, so it cannot be evolution. Only populations have a gene pool whose frequencies can shift. Evolution happens to the population, not to the body.

questions.question: Mutations supply all new variation, yet mutation alone is considered a weak force in evolution. Why?
questions.solution: Mutation rates per gene are low, and most mutations are neutral or deleterious, so mutation slowly dribbles in variation with negligible directional effect on frequencies. Selection, drift and gene flow change frequencies much faster. Mutation is the ultimate SOURCE of variation but not the mechanism of change — it stocks the shelf, others decide what sells.

questions.question: Selection favours taller individuals, but if height is purely environmental the population will not change. Why is heritability the crucial condition?
questions.solution: Selection acts on phenotypes; evolution requires that the phenotype difference be passed on. If height variation is due to nutrition only, the tall individuals' offspring are not taller than average, so no frequency shift occurs. Response to selection = heritability × selection differential. Selection needs a heritable component, or it changes nothing in the next generation.
